label: Clothes and shoes
rationale: The everyday on/off pairs for what you're dressed in: clothes go on with kiru, shoes with haku, and both come off with nugu.
mixUps: kiru vs haku: kiru for the torso or whole body, haku for anything you step into; nugu takes both off, so drill kiru/haku against the one nugu (fuku kite / kutsu haite / kutsu nuide).

targets.verbSense: put on or wear on the body (tops, coats, dresses)
targets.trap: kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which take other verbs (haku, kaburu, kakeru).
targets.use: Mostly heard as kiteru (is wearing, a state, not 'putting on now') or kiteku (wear when going out); casual speech drops o. kiteru 'wearing' is flat (ki-TE-RU) while kiteru 'has come' falls after ki (KI-te-ru), so pitch as well as context tells them apart.
targets.notes: Off: fuku o nugu. Changing into other clothes is fuku o kigaeru; looking good in them is fuku ga niau (niau ne).

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa donna fuku o kite ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はどんな服を着ていきますか？

targets.verbSense: put on or wear on the feet and legs
targets.trap: Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.
targets.use: Said as kutsu haite (put your shoes on) at the door; casual speech drops o. haiteru means already has them on, not 'putting them on now'.
targets.notes: Spelled like haku 'throw up' and haku 'sweep', but the pitch differs: haku 'put on' is flat (ha-KU), the other two fall after ha (HA-ku). Context helps too.

example.romaji: chotto matte, ima kutsu haku kara.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、今靴履くから。
example.english: Hang on, I'm putting my shoes on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima kutsu o hakimasu node, chotto matte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今靴を履きますので、ちょっと待ってください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm just putting my shoes on, one moment please.

targets.trap: Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.
targets.use: Heard as kutsu nuide (kudasai) at home entrances, some restaurants and clinics. Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: A hat comes off with boushi o toru or nugu; glasses and accessories with hazusu.

example.english: Take your shoes off here, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de kutsu o nuide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここで靴を脱いでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please take your shoes off here.

targets.trap: Not fuku o toru, which sounds like picking clothes up (fuku totte = pass me my clothes). Whatever goes on with kiru or haku (tops, trousers, shoes, socks) comes off with nugu. A hat comes off with toru or nugu. Glasses, masks, watches, ties and belts come off with hazusu, and casual toru works for most of them.
targets.use: Heard as nuide (take them off) or nuida hou ga ii (you'd better take them off), and ofuku nuide (with the o- used to children) is what kids hear at bath time. When it's one layer, people name it: uwagi nuidara? (why not take your jacket off?). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Once it's clear which garment, nugu alone is enough: atsui kara nuijaou (it's hot, I'll take it off).

example.romaji: nureta fuku, hayaku nuida hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 濡れた服、早く脱いだ方がいいよ。
example.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.

examplePolite.romaji: nureta fuku wa, hayaku nuida hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 濡れた服は、早く脱いだ方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.
